## FSD1 · FSD1-fid-rename — FSD1: what a fid rests on across a rename, and where a file's id comes from

Status: **resolved** · Assigned to: Architect · Revision: 6

Evidence: Ruled by architect-8 (.wash/local/FSD1-fid-rename-ruling.md): (A) a fid is {path, id}, re-resolved and checked on every op, removed when gone or another id, fids do not follow renames; red's BLOCK closed by construction: a create moves the counter in one commit then creates the entry with its id attribute in its creating commit (littlefs's creating open and mkdir take initial attributes), so no read path writes and no id-less entry can exist; mount checks ids without writing (every entry has one, no duplicates, counter above the highest) else corrupt. Tests listed in the ruling; page lines in FSD1's commit; forwarded to FSD1's implementer.

### Orchestrator · Question

Event: `9ea9dc8afc658ecec8666a255caaab08` · 2026-10-03T06:18:37Z

> From FSD1's implementer (fsd.md 'Volumes, connections and labels', brief rule 5): littlefs exposes no stable inode number and a skeleton node holds no resource and is dropped unseen, so fsd cannot refcount an id -> location table. (A, recommended by both of us): a node is {path from the root, built only from client walk names; file id}, the id fsd's own attribute (type 0, a u64 from a never-reused counter on the root's attribute, also qid.path); every op resolves the path and checks the id, and absent or different means `removed`; the id is the generation, so a remove or a rename-over ends it for every other fid; a fid on a renamed file, or anything below a renamed directory (a minted connection's root included), also reads `removed`. No table, no memory beyond the fid. (B): fids follow renames via an id -> (parent id, name) table for every node handed out this mount, Plan 9's semantics, memory scaling with the volume since nodes die unseen. Either way: a file with no id attribute (another implementation, or a hostile medium) is served as `corrupt`, never assigned one on a read path; attribute numbering 0 id, 1 mtime, 2 qid version, the root's next-id counter type 3. The implementer builds toward its checkpoint on (A); only node resolution changes if you rule (B). Your ruling and the page line; if you are at your handoff, pass it to architect-8 in the handoff.

Event: `f5233265fc235d43f36f68349babaf9a` · 2026-10-03T06:20:05Z

> Correction from the implementer to the corrupt rule: littlefs commits a create and its attributes separately, so a power cut between them leaves an honest id-less entry. Revised (A): fsd gives an id-less entry its id the first time it hands out a node for it (walk, create, directory listing), as finishing the interrupted create; a volume that cannot be written then answers corrupt for that entry. Same under (B). Rule with this in hand.

### Orchestrator · Question

Event: `347c00fb7ee7ade799a3cddd1f8b215d` · 2026-10-03T06:42:13Z

> Red's review of FSD1 (BLOCK) bears on this ruling: giving an id-less entry its id on first touch (walk, directory listing) WRITES the volume on a read path, so a caller with read-only access (labels a strict superset of the volume's) writes the root's next-id counter and the entry's id, breaking R25 and fsd.md:57 (a write needs equal labels) - and equal-label clients then see the counter in their next create's qid.path, a channel from a higher reader down. Red's fix options: give the id only after a Write check, or serve the entry without writing. The second P1 is separate and fixable now (blkd ranges' read_only flag dropped; a refused write poisons the volume as corrupt for everyone; a blank read-only range is formatted). P2s: ATTR_NEXT_ID trusted from the medium (a counter below a live id gives a duplicate); NoSpace in give_id makes an id-less entry unwalkable. So the ruling needs one more clause: what a reader sees for an id-less entry (my lean: serve it read-only with no id - a transient node that cannot be written, renamed or removed through that fid, and no persistent id is minted until a caller with write access touches it; the counter is validated at mount against the highest id present, or the volume is corrupt). Rule (A)/(B) and this together; FSD1's fix round waits on it for this item only.

### Architect · Answer

Event: `541edc83f1754771433fb4e362905e1d` · 2026-10-03T06:47:31Z

> Ruling (architect-8); detail, tests and exact fsd.md lines: .wash/local/FSD1-fid-rename-ruling.md.
> 
> 1. (A): a fid is {path, id}; every op re-resolves the path and checks the id; gone or other id = `removed`; fids do not follow renames. (B)'s table grows with every node a client walks to, keyed on a number littlefs lacks; no page promises Plan 9's rename-following.
> 
> 2. Reader clause: neither "id on first touch" nor transient nodes. Remove the source of id-less entries instead: a create moves the root's counter in one commit, then creates the entry WITH its id attribute in its creating commit (a small littlefs addition: mkdir and a creating open take initial user attributes, same tag list). A power cut burns an id, never leaves an entry without one. Nothing but a create (equal labels) moves the counter, so no read path writes: red's BLOCK (R25, fsd.md:57) is closed by construction.
> 
> 3. Mount checks ids without writing: every entry has an id, no duplicates, counter above the highest; otherwise the volume is served as corrupt under the existing Mounting rule. fsd serves only volumes it wrote. This closes red's P2s (counter trusted; NoSpace stranding an entry). give_id, TRANSIENT and find's transient arm go.
> 
> Tests owed: crash-at-every-write over create-with-attributes; a power cut mid-rename across pairs still passes the mount check (pending move not counted twice); reads by a higher-labelled caller write nothing; id-less / duplicate / low-counter images are corrupt; renamed-file and below-renamed-dir fids get `removed`.
> 
> Red's other P1 (blkd read_only dropped) is separate and unchanged by this; a read-only range now serves with no write at all.
> 
> Not an owner choice: follows from R25, R49, the Mounting rule and tenet 1. Page lines go in FSD1's commit as written in the file. Returning the thread to you.
